name: Budget and Enrollment Forecasting
title: Budget and Enrollment Forecasting
answer: Budget and enrollment forecasting uses models, often aided by AI, to predict how many students will enroll in each school and grade, because funding usually follows students. Forecasts should be presented as a range rather than a single number, and budget scenarios help boards see the effects of different choices. People, not the models, make the final decisions.

sections.body: Budgets depend on enrollment forecasts, since funding often follows students. Demographers and planners use models to predict how many students will enroll in each school and grade, and AI can help analyze trends in births, housing, and migration. The problem this solves is that districts must plan finances without knowing future enrollment, so forecasts give them a basis for budgeting. Forecasts should always come with a range, not a single number, since the future is uncertain. Budget scenarios then help boards see the effects of choices.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: A finance office can use spreadsheet tools with AI to model what happens if enrollment falls, state funding changes, or costs rise. These scenarios inform decisions, but people make them, and boards should understand the assumptions behind each scenario. The text does not give separate grade band examples for this idea. Districts should also compare past forecasts with what actually happened to learn how reliable they are. That record helps boards judge how much weight to give new forecasts.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It states plainly that forecasts can be wrong, sometimes badly, and that a forecast built on past trends may miss a new housing development or a change in state policy. The recommended check is practical: compare past forecasts with what actually happened to learn how reliable they are. This idea therefore rests on practice rather than research as presented in the text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Forecasts can be wrong, sometimes badly, and a forecast built on past trends may miss a new housing development or a change in state policy. Forecasts should always come with a range, not a single number, since the future is uncertain. The scenarios inform decisions, but people make them, and boards should understand the assumptions behind each scenario. Districts should compare past forecasts with what actually happened to learn how reliable they are, and that record helps boards judge how much weight to give new forecasts. The decisions stay with people, not the models.
